entries.title: How a 13th-Century Monk Created a Prayer Manuscript by Writing Over—and Accidentally Preserving—Archimedes’ Groundbreaking Mathematical Works
entries.summary: In Jerusalem of the year 1229, there lived a Greek Orthodox monk named Johannes Myronas. Needing some parchment for a prayer book, he grabbed some already-used pages, erased their existing content, and over them wrote down “prayers for the dead, prayers for repentance, blessings for the loaves at Easter, and even a prayer for those […]
entries.content:
In Jerusalem of the year 1229, there lived a Greek Ortho­dox monk named Johannes Myronas. Need­ing some parch­ment for a prayer book, he grabbed some already-used pages, erased their exist­ing con­tent, and over them wrote down “prayers for the dead, prayers for repen­tance, bless­ings for the loaves at East­er, and even a prayer for those who were unrea­son­ably exclud­ed,” says math-and-sci­ence YouTu­ber Ben Syversen in the video above. Myronas may have ful­filled his reli­gious duty with­out using too much valu­able parch­ment, but he could­n’t have known the even greater rel­e­vance his actions would turn out to have had in the realm of math­e­mat­ics. For the pages he’d scrubbed were a Greek com­pi­la­tion con­tain­ing the only known copy of cer­tain works by the ancient poly­math Archimedes.

As it turns out, Myronas com­mit­ted per­haps the most notable act of inad­ver­tent preser­va­tion in the his­to­ry of math­e­mat­ics. We get the word palimpsest from the medieval prac­tice of over­writ­ing a page after first eras­ing what had been on it before, though incom­plete­ly; hence the mean­ing of mul­ti­ple lay­ers that have remained leg­i­ble over time.

In the case of what we now know as the Archimedes Palimpsest, that leg­i­bil­i­ty was achieved only with the aid of late twen­ti­eth-cen­tu­ry and ear­ly twen­ty-first-cen­tu­ry tech­nol­o­gy, in addi­tion to the painstak­ing con­ser­va­tion effort required to keep this tenth-cen­tu­ry doc­u­ment in more or less one piece. (And all of that was only pos­si­ble thanks to the epic his­tor­i­cal jour­ney the Palimpsest took, which end­ed in 1998 when it sold for $2 mil­lion at Christie’s to a tech fig­ure we’re only assured is not Bill Gates.)

You can learn more about that project from the TED Talk just above by its direc­tor, the late William Noel of Bal­ti­more’s Wal­ters Art Muse­um. Thanks to his ded­i­ca­tion and that of his team, we now have writ­ings of Archimedes like the Stom­a­chion, which deals with a kind of chil­dren’s puz­zle that turns out to have con­sid­er­able sim­i­lar­i­ties with an ear­ly prob­lem in the field of com­bi­na­torics, and more impor­tant­ly, The Method of Mechan­i­cal The­o­rems, an expla­na­tion of cal­cu­lus-like pro­ce­dures for deter­min­ing area or vol­ume. None of this proves that Archimedes was the inven­tor of com­bi­na­torics or cal­cu­lus, exact­ly, but it does show us just how much fur­ther he’d man­aged to push Greek math­e­mat­ics than we’d pre­vi­ous­ly known. Besides, any work that can bring togeth­er his­to­ri­ans, clas­si­cists, math­e­mati­cians, con­ser­va­tors, physi­cists, and com­put­er sci­en­tists more than two mil­len­nia after its com­po­si­tion sure­ly mer­its a place in the canon.

entries.title: Hear What Homer’s Odyssey Sounded Like When Sung in the Original Ancient Greek
entries.summary: Image via Wikimedia Commons It’s been a humanist truism for some time to say that Shakespeare speaks to every age, transcending his time and place through the sheer force of his universal genius. But any honest student first encountering the plays will tell you differently, as will many a seasoned scholar who works hard to […]
entries.content:
Image via Wiki­me­dia Com­mons

It’s been a human­ist tru­ism for some time to say that Shake­speare speaks to every age, tran­scend­ing his time and place through the sheer force of his uni­ver­sal genius. But any hon­est stu­dent first encoun­ter­ing the plays will tell you dif­fer­ent­ly, as will many a sea­soned schol­ar who works hard to place the writer and his work in his­tor­i­cal con­text. Even one­time direc­tor of London’s Nation­al The­atre, Nicholas Hyt­ner, once said, “I’ll admit that I hard­ly ever go to a per­for­mance of one of Shakespeare’s plays with­out expe­ri­enc­ing blind pan­ic dur­ing the first five min­utes. I sit there think­ing… I have no idea what these peo­ple are talk­ing about.”

Of course, none of that means we can’t learn to appre­ci­ate Shake­speare, and we do not need a grad­u­ate-lev­el edu­ca­tion to do so. But much of his archa­ic lan­guage and obscure ref­er­ences will always sound for­eign to mod­ern ears. How much more so, then, the lan­guage of the ancient Greeks, whether in trans­la­tion or not? Although we’ve also been taught to think of the Home­r­ic epics as con­tain­ers of uni­ver­sal truth and beau­ty, the world of Homer was, in many ways, an alien one—and the lit­er­a­ture of ancient Greece was far clos­er to song than even Shakespeare’s musi­cal speech­es.

In fact, “before writ­ing was gen­er­al­ly known among the Greeks,” the Uni­ver­si­ty of Cincin­nati notes, “poets recit­ed and sang sto­ries for audi­ences at the courts of city lead­ers and at fes­ti­vals. A poet could actu­al­ly impro­vise a tale in the six-beat rhythm of Greek verse if he knew the plot of his sto­ry.” We do not know whether Homer was one enter­pris­ing scribe or “a group of poets whose works on the theme of Troy were col­lect­ed” under one name. But in either case, that poet or poets heard the tales of Hec­tor and Achilles, Odysseus and Pene­lope, and all those med­dling gods sung before they wrote them down. Now, thanks to Georg Danek of the Uni­ver­si­ty of Vien­na and Ste­fan Hagel of the Aus­tri­an Acad­e­my of Sci­ences, we have some idea of what those songs may have sound­ed like.

“In the course of the last years,” write Danek and Hagel, “we have devel­oped a tech­nique of singing the Home­r­ic epics, which is appro­pri­ate for the pri­mar­i­ly oral tra­di­tion from which these poems emerge.” The two schol­ars cau­tion that their the­o­ret­i­cal recre­ations are “not to be under­stood as the exact recon­struc­tion of a giv­en melody, but as an approach to the tech­nique the Home­r­ic singers used to accom­mo­date melod­ic prin­ci­ples to the demands of the indi­vid­ual verse.” Accom­pa­nied by a four-stringed lyre-like instru­ment called a phorminx, “the Home­r­ic bard” would impro­vise the “melody at the same time as he impro­vised his text, which was unique in every per­for­mance.” In the audio above, you can hear Danek and Hagel’s melod­ic recre­ation of lines 267–366 of book 8 of the Odyssey, in which Demod­ocus sings about the love of Ares and Aphrodite.

At their site, the two schol­ars present an abstract of their Home­r­ic singing the­o­ry, with musi­co­log­i­cal and lin­guis­tic evi­dence for the recre­ation. Their tech­ni­cal cri­te­ria will con­fuse the non-spe­cial­ist, and none but ancient Greek speak­ers will under­stand the record­ing above. But it brings us a lit­tle clos­er to expe­ri­enc­ing Home­r’s epic poet­ry, “the foun­da­tion stones of Euro­pean Lit­er­a­ture,” as the ancient Greeks might have expe­ri­enced it.

If you would like to sup­port the mis­sion of Open Cul­ture, con­sid­er mak­ing a dona­tion to our site. It’s hard to rely 100% on ads, and your con­tri­bu­tions will help us con­tin­ue pro­vid­ing the best free cul­tur­al and edu­ca­tion­al mate­ri­als to learn­ers every­where. You can con­tribute through Pay­Pal, Patre­on, and Ven­mo (@openculture). Thanks!

Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2016.

entries.title: What Miles Davis Taught Herbie Hancock: In Music, as in Life, There Are No Mistakes, Just Chances to Improvise
entries.summary: One of my favorite Brian Eno quotes, or rather one that became an Oblique Strategy, is “Honor Your Mistake as a Hidden Intention.” (Or to be pedantic, the original version was “Honor Thy Error…”). As a teenager growing up and trying to make art (at that time music and comics) there was no advice more […]
entries.content:
One of my favorite Bri­an Eno quotes, or rather one that became an Oblique Strat­e­gy, is “Hon­or Your Mis­take as a Hid­den Inten­tion.” (Or to be pedan­tic, the orig­i­nal ver­sion was “Hon­or Thy Error…”).

As a teenag­er grow­ing up and try­ing to make art (at that time music and comics) there was no advice more free­ing. It was the oppo­site of what I thought I knew: mis­takes were shame­ful, the sign of an ama­teur or of the lack of prac­tice. But the more art I made, the more I ref­er­enced Eno’s idea, and the more I read and lis­tened, the more I real­ized it wasn’t just Eno.

The Bea­t­les left in an alarm clock meant for the musi­cians on “A Day in the Life” and the sound of emp­ty booze bot­tles vibrat­ing on a speak­er was left in at the end of “Long Long Long” (along with tons more). The Beast­ie Boys left in a jump­ing nee­dle intend­ed for a smooth scratch on “The Sounds of Sci­ence.” Radio­head left in Jon­ny Greenwood’s warm-up chord that became essen­tial to “Creep.” (There’s a whole Red­dit thread devot­ed to these mis­takes if you choose to go down the rab­bit hole.)

But those exam­ples relate to the record­ing process of rock music. What about jazz? Sure­ly there are “wrong” notes when it comes to play­ing, espe­cial­ly if you’re not the soloist.

In this very short video based around an inter­view with pianist Her­bie Han­cock, the mas­ter impro­vis­er Miles Davis hon­ored Hancock’s mis­take as a hid­den inten­tion by play­ing along with it. It’s both a sur­pris­ing look into the arcane world of jazz impro­vi­sa­tion and a reveal­ing anec­dote of Davis, usu­al­ly known as a dif­fi­cult col­lab­o­ra­tor.

“It taught me a very big les­son not only about music,” says Han­cock, “but about life.”

Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2016.

entries.title: Christopher Hitchens Explains Why Homer’s Odyssey Still Matters to Our World (2000)
entries.summary: At the moment, the answer to the question of why we should read Homer’s Odyssey seems rather straightforward: so we can more intelligently voice our opinions on Christopher Nolan’s new blockbuster film adaptation. A quarter-century ago, the matter was somewhat less clear. Still, an occasion had presented itself in the form of a new English translation, […]
entries.content:
At the moment, the answer to the ques­tion of why we should read Home­r’s Odyssey seems rather straight­for­ward: so we can more intel­li­gent­ly voice our opin­ions on Christo­pher Nolan’s new block­buster film adap­ta­tion. A quar­ter-cen­tu­ry ago, the mat­ter was some­what less clear. Still, an occa­sion had pre­sent­ed itself in the form of a new Eng­lish trans­la­tion, by Uni­ver­si­ty of Kansas clas­sics pro­fes­sor Stan­ley Lom­bar­do. That book, and the work of Homer in gen­er­al, was the sub­ject of a live two-hour round­table dis­cus­sion aired on C‑SPAN’s Book TV in the fall of 2000, which, with the Odyssey back in the zeit­geist, appeared on YouTube just days ago.

Apart from Lom­bar­do him­self, the par­tic­i­pants include Joseph Bot­tum, then lit­er­ary edi­tor of the Week­ly Stan­dard; jour­nal­ist and mil­i­tary vet­er­an Debra J. Dick­er­son; and Christo­pher Hitchens, who clear­ly par­tic­i­pat­ed not just because he hap­pened to be liv­ing in Wash­ing­ton, D.C., but also out of a gen­uine appre­ci­a­tion for the Odyssey and an under­stand­ing of its rel­e­vance in the mod­ern world. Ear­ly on in the text, he explains, Homer intro­duces the con­cepts of hubris and neme­sis, which “we can­not do with­out in ordi­nary dis­course. There are cer­tain pun­ish­ments that appear to fall on peo­ple, for orig­i­nal arro­gance or con­ceit, that we can’t con­ceive of relat­ing grand sto­ries with­out.”

There’s the “caprice of the gods,” with which every reli­gion has had to deal, as well as the even more uni­ver­sal feel­ing of nos­tal­gia, “a very overused and sen­ti­men­tal­ized term now, which lit­er­al­ly means — and can only real­ly mean — the yearn­ing to go home.” Adduc­ing such re-inter­pre­ta­tions by writ­ers from Alexan­der Pope to James Joyce, Hitchens declares that we think of the Odyssey as “the orig­i­nal nar­ra­tive of the striv­ing of human­i­ty — and of the need, also, to beware of what you want, in case you ever do, as Cavafy says, final­ly get home to Itha­ca. It may turn out that it’s bet­ter to trav­el hope­ful­ly than to arrive.”

The mat­ter of virtue also aris­es in the con­ver­sa­tion, and specif­i­cal­ly whether the range of virtues of which Homer sang (up to and includ­ing luck) would be rec­og­nized in our Chris­t­ian or post-Chris­t­ian world. To the avowed­ly athe­ist Hitchens’ mind, of course, we should already have been post-reli­gious. Home­r’s deities are “anthro­po­mor­phic gods; they are invent­ed by us, as all gods are.” But what­ev­er your reli­gion or lack there­of, “if you don’t know some­thing about clas­si­cal Greece, then you won’t be able, with much prof­it, to read Shake­speare, or Mil­ton, or Shel­ley, or Keats, or even Chaucer. It would be like not know­ing what the bible sto­ry was and then won­der­ing how you puz­zle your way through Shake­speare as well. It’s part of the under­lay; it’s part of the com­mon her­itage.” The trans­la­tions and re-inter­pre­ta­tions have kept com­ing, but Homer him­self still patient­ly awaits each of us.

entries.title: Christopher Nolan Picks 15 Favorite Films from the Criterion Closet
entries.summary: Maybe you’ve already seen Christopher Nolan’s new cinematic interpretation of the Odyssey more than once; maybe you don’t know whether you’ll ever get around to it at all. Either way, you’ve got to admit that the man makes films in a way very few living directors do. His combination of blockbuster-scale spectacle and personal vision, a […]
entries.content:
Maybe you’ve already seen Christo­pher Nolan’s new cin­e­mat­ic inter­pre­ta­tion of the Odyssey more than once; maybe you don’t know whether you’ll ever get around to it at all. Either way, you’ve got to admit that the man makes films in a way very few liv­ing direc­tors do. His com­bi­na­tion of block­buster-scale spec­ta­cle and per­son­al vision, a rare expe­ri­ence indeed at the the­ater these days, can real­ly only be achieved by film­mak­ers with a thor­ough­go­ing love of the medi­um. Most of us will require no fur­ther proof of that love than this new video cap­tur­ing his vis­it to the Cri­te­ri­on Clos­et, that both hal­lowed and much-YouTubed space jam-packed with releas­es from the most wide­ly known home-video brand for cinephiles.

Unsur­pris­ing­ly, it’s not his first vis­it. “Last time I was here, there were no cam­eras, and I got to just come and steal some films,” he says, “but now I’m singing for my sup­per.” Unlike some film­mak­ers, he does­n’t play it cool for the audi­ence; rather, he imme­di­ate­ly starts pulling down Don Siegel’s neo-noir Hem­ing­way adap­ta­tion The Killers, a five-pic­ture John Cas­savetes box set, and Al Rein­ert’s Bri­an Eno-scored NASA doc­u­men­tary For All Mankind. It’s not a sur­prise to see him go for an Orson Welles movie, but the one that first catch­es his eye is Mr. Arkadin, which Welles “made all over the world in the scrap­pi­est, most sort of home­made, put-his-friends-togeth­er, grab-some-cos­tumes, find-an-inter­est­ing-loca­tion kind of way.”

Fritz Lang’s The Tes­ta­ment of Dr. Mabuse, he recalls, pro­vid­ed him and his broth­er-col­lab­o­ra­tor inspi­ra­tion for the Jok­er as famous­ly por­trayed by Heath Ledger in The Dark Knight. The com­plete Apu tril­o­gy by Satya­jit Ray reminds him that, how­ev­er great an impact the first of those films made on him, he nev­er did watch the oth­er two. For many movie­go­ers in the Eng­lish-speak­ing world of the mid-twen­ti­eth cen­tu­ry, Ray’s work was some of the first “world cin­e­ma” they’d ever seen; Nolan’s fel­low cinephile-auteur Mar­tin Scors­ese has done his part to bol­ster that tra­di­tion with his World Cin­e­ma Project series, and Nolan pulls off the shelf one of its vol­umes fea­tur­ing pic­tures from Cuba, Indone­sia, Iran, and else­where.

Though tech­ni­cal­ly British, Nolan is the par­tial­ly Chica­go-raised son of an Amer­i­can moth­er long since accept­ed as a kind of Hol­ly­wood native. His taste in movies, too, reflects a streak of high Amer­i­can­ism, which man­i­fests in selec­tions like Spike Lee’s Mal­colm X, David Lynch’s Lost High­way, Carl Franklin’s One False Move, and Richard Lin­klater’s Boy­hood. (As for Robert Alt­man’s satir­i­cal thriller The Play­er, it would be hard to imag­ine how he could­n’t appre­ci­ate its wicked­ly inci­sive depic­tion of “the Indus­try.”) Com­ing to the end of his Clos­et time, he also man­ages to grab God­frey Reg­gio’s Qat­si tril­o­gy, which con­sti­tutes “one of the great pieces of pure cin­e­ma,” and Car­roll Bal­lard’s The Black Stal­lion, a child­hood favorite that stayed with him. Like all the most suc­cess­ful film­mak­ers, Nolan under­stands that you’ve got to end strong, and in a way that does­n’t require expla­na­tion: hence, per­haps, his final choice of Cit­i­zen Kane.

entries.title: The Essence of Hayao Miyazaki Films: A Short Documentary About the Humanity at the Heart of His Animation
entries.summary: Filmmaker Hayao Miyazaki detests being referred to as the Japanese Walt Disney. The great animator and storyteller admires the gorgeous animation of classic Disney films, but finds them lacking in emotional complexity, the element he prizes above all else. Miyazaki’s films are celebrated for their mystical, supernatural elements, but they take shape around the human characters […]
entries.content:
Film­mak­er Hayao Miyaza­ki detests being referred to as the Japan­ese Walt Dis­ney. The great ani­ma­tor and sto­ry­teller admires the gor­geous ani­ma­tion of clas­sic Dis­ney films, but finds them lack­ing in emo­tion­al com­plex­i­ty, the ele­ment he prizes above all else.

Miyaza­k­i’s films are cel­e­brat­ed for their mys­ti­cal, super­nat­ur­al ele­ments, but they take shape around the human char­ac­ters inhab­it­ing them. Plot comes lat­er, after he has fig­ured out the desires dri­ving his peo­ple. “Keep it sim­ple,” he coun­sels in Lewis Bond’s short doc­u­men­tary The Essence of Human­i­ty above. An inter­est­ing piece of advice, giv­en that a hall­mark of his 60-year career is his insis­tence on cre­at­ing real­is­tic three-dimen­sion­al char­ac­ters, warts and all.

Amer­i­can ani­ma­tors are also taught to sim­pli­fy. They should all be able to sum up the essence of their pro­posed fea­tures by fill­ing in the blank of the phrase “I want _____,” pre­sum­ably because such con­ci­sion is a nec­es­sary ele­ment of a suc­cess­ful ele­va­tor pitch.

As Bond points out, West­ern ani­mat­ed fea­tures often end with a con­ve­nient deus ex machi­na, free­ing the char­ac­ters up for a crowd-pleas­ing dance par­ty as the cred­its roll.

Miyaza­ki doesn’t cot­ton to the idea of tidy, unearned end­ings, nor does he feel bound to grant his char­ac­ters their wants, pre­fer­ring instead to give them what they need. Spir­i­tu­al growth is supe­ri­or to wish ful­fill­ment here.

Such growth rarely hap­pens with­out time for reflec­tion, and Miyaza­ki films are notable for the num­ber of non-ver­bal scenes where­in char­ac­ters per­form small, every­day actions, a num­ber of which can be sam­pled in Bond’s doc­u­men­tary. The beau­ti­ful­ly ren­dered weath­er and set­tings have pro­vid­ed clues as to the char­ac­ters’ devel­op­ment, ever since the love­ly scene of cloud shad­ows skim­ming across a field in his first fea­ture, 1979’s The Cas­tle of Cagliostro.

Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2015.

entries.title: Where Did Europe’s Countries—and the United Kingdom—Get Their Names?
entries.summary: The typical student traveling on a Eurail pass will stop in such lands as Österreich, Italia, Česko and Schweiz — also known as Suisse, Svizzera, and Svizra. If that student happens to hail from the English-speaking world, the names Austria, Italy, the Czech Republic (the recent movement for Czechia notwithstanding), and Switzerland will sound more familiar. But […]
entries.content:
The typ­i­cal stu­dent trav­el­ing on a Eurail pass will stop in such lands as Öster­re­ich, Italia, Česko and Schweiz — also known as Suisse, Svizzera, and Svizra. If that stu­dent hap­pens to hail from the Eng­lish-speak­ing world, the names Aus­tria, Italy, the Czech Repub­lic (the recent move­ment for Czechia notwith­stand­ing), and Switzer­land will sound more famil­iar. But the ques­tion inevitably comes to mind while rid­ing between one his­tor­i­cal­ly and cul­tur­al­ly rich cap­i­tal to anoth­er: where did all these coun­tries get their names in Eng­lish? How on Earth, for exam­ple, did Deutsch­land, known in cer­tain oth­er Euro­pean lan­guages as Alle­magne, Ale­ma­nia, or Ale­man­ha, get to be called Ger­many?

Lan­guage YouTu­ber Rob­Words has an expla­na­tion. “To the Romans, it was the land of the Ger­mani, their name for the weird peo­ple speak­ing gib­ber­ish lan­guages to the east of the Riv­er Rhine,” he says in the video above, stand­ing in a for­est con­ve­nient­ly locat­ed in Ger­many itself.

They “also used the word ale­man­ni to describe a con­fed­er­a­tion of Ger­man­ic peo­ple, and that’s where a load of oth­er lan­guages get their word for Ger­many too.” And the mean­ing of Deutsch­land? “Land of the Dutch,” that last actu­al­ly being the descen­dant of an old Ger­man­ic word mean­ing ‘pop­u­lar’ or ‘peo­ple’ ” — which, before that time, referred not sim­ply to human beings, but the pop­u­la­tion who spoke the region’s wide­ly under­stood “pop­u­lar lan­guages.”

Behind most every Euro­pean coun­try’s Eng­lish name lies a sto­ry, if some­times an ambigu­ous, con­test­ed, and con­tro­ver­sial one. Most are also his­tor­i­cal­ly illu­mi­nat­ing: take Bel­gium, once con­sid­ered part of the Nether­lands (home of the peo­ple we now call Dutch), whose name derives from a tribe, or con­fed­er­a­tion of tribes, known in Latin as the Bel­gae: a word “adopt­ed by peo­ple liv­ing in the south­ern Low Coun­tries dur­ing the region’s strug­gle for inde­pen­dence from Spain in the six­teenth cen­tu­ry.” Rob­Words has more such sur­pris­ing facts to reveal in the video just above, in which he breaks down the names of all the coun­tries in the Unit­ed King­dom, cov­er­ing Ire­land, Scot­land, Wales, his native Eng­land, and also the word Britain itself, as well as the Great often attached to it. The lat­ter isn’t a boast, he stress­es, but rather a means of dis­tin­guish­ing the island from part of France. As for which part, you’ll have to watch to find out.

entries.title: 19th Century Japanese Woodblock Prints Creatively Illustrate the Inner Workings of the Human Body
entries.summary: Folks with a passing knowledge of ukiyo‑e, the Japanese woodblock print art form popular in the 17th through 19th centuries, will be familiar with its landscapes, as well as its portraits of courtesans and kabuki actors. But often these prints were educational, as demonstrated by these very odd anatomical prints that promote good health as […]
entries.content:
Folks with a pass­ing knowl­edge of ukiyo‑e, the Japan­ese wood­block print art form pop­u­lar in the 17th through 19th cen­turies, will be famil­iar with its land­scapes, as well as its por­traits of cour­te­sans and kabu­ki actors. But often these prints were edu­ca­tion­al, as demon­strat­ed by these very odd anatom­i­cal prints that pro­mote good health as it relates to our inter­nal work­ings.

Long before ani­mat­ed mon­sters warned us about our mucus-filled chests, Japan­ese artists like Uta­gawa Kunisa­da (1786–1865) filled the guts of these men and women with lit­tle work­ers, mak­ing sure the human body worked like a func­tion­ing vil­lage or town.

In the first print, Inshoku Yojo Kaga­mi (“Mir­ror of the Phys­i­ol­o­gy of Drink­ing and Eat­ing”), a man dines on fish and drinks sake. Inside, lit­tle men scur­ry about a pool wrapped in intestines, stoke a fire under the heart, all the while a schol­ar keeps ref­er­ence mate­ri­als near­by. Down below lone­ly fig­ures guard the “urine gate” and the “feces gate,” sure­ly one of the worst jobs in all the body econ­o­my.

One of Kunisada’s stu­dents cre­at­ed a print for the women, focus­ing on the repro­duc­tive organs, called Boji Yojo Kaga­mi (“Rules of Sex­u­al Life”). Keen-eyed view­ers will note that the minia­ture work­ers here are all women, so at least there’s some equal­i­ty at play.

The two prints were meant as instruc­tion­al, point­ing out best health prac­tices, and warn­ing against overindul­gence and excess.

Oth­er prints are just as inven­tive: a back and abdomen cov­ered in chil­dren play­ing famil­iar games; anoth­er fea­tur­ing pop­u­lar kabu­ki actors stand­ing in for var­i­ous organs. (Now, that is just cry­ing out for a mod­ern remake). The last print shows a preg­nant woman whose bel­ly con­tains Tainai jukkai no zu (Ten Realms with­in the body), a Bud­dhist idea that you can read more about here. As for their func­tion inside the womb, that is for oth­ers of a high­er con­scious­ness to dis­cern.

Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2019.

Relat­ed Con­tent:

Ted Mills is a free­lance writer on the arts.

entries.title: A Free Online Archive Lets You Explore 5.8 Million Works of Art Spanning 5,000 Years of History
entries.summary: Though it’s traditionally meant “last in a progression or series,” as Merriam-Webster puts it, the word ultimate has been more often used in recent decades to mean “the best or most extreme of its kind.” The name of a recently launched digital archive performs a rare inversion, labeling as last a creation marked not by finality but extremity. Billed as “the […]
entries.content:
Though it’s tra­di­tion­al­ly meant “last in a pro­gres­sion or series,” as Mer­ri­am-Web­ster puts it, the word ulti­mate has been more often used in recent decades to mean “the best or most extreme of its kind.” The name of a recent­ly launched dig­i­tal archive per­forms a rare inver­sion, label­ing as last a cre­ation marked not by final­i­ty but extrem­i­ty. Billed as “the largest search engine for muse­um art,” The Last Muse­um cur­rent­ly index­es around five mil­lion art­works, both those in the pub­lic domain and those cov­ered by fair use. What­ev­er sort of art you wish to see, just describe it in the search bar, hit enter, and enjoy the numer­ous and diverse results from through­out his­to­ry and all around the world.

“Rather than func­tion­ing as a muse­um itself, the web­site aggre­gates pub­licly avail­able col­lec­tion records and images from thou­sands of insti­tu­tions, allow­ing vis­i­tors to explore every­thing from Old Mas­ter paint­ings and ancient Egypt­ian sculp­ture to Japan­ese wood­block prints and vin­tage comics in one place,” writes Sage Helene at My Mod­ern Met.

“Vis­i­tors can search by themes, moods, col­ors, sub­jects, or descrip­tive phras­es with­out know­ing an artwork’s title or artist. The sys­tem iden­ti­fies relat­ed con­cepts and returns visu­al­ly and the­mat­i­cal­ly con­nect­ed works, mak­ing it easy to dis­cov­er unex­pect­ed pieces across cul­tures, time peri­ods, and col­lec­tions.” Its cre­ators under­stand that the val­ue of search lies in not just effi­cien­cy, but also sur­prise — not that the user expe­ri­ence is entire­ly “vibes-based,” as the kids today might say.

Though the search results can come, by default, from any time between 3000 BC and the cur­rent year, you can nar­row the his­tor­i­cal range by drag­ging the ends of the blue time­line inward. And if you pre­fer more spe­cif­ic brows­ing, you can also nav­i­gate through its lists of cul­tures or muse­ums.  The for­mer includes every­thing from French, Roman, and Japan­ese (with a strong selec­tion of wood­block prints), to Cham­pa, Tajik, and Basque. The lat­ter includes the British Muse­um, the Rijksmu­se­um, and the Met­ro­pol­i­tan Muse­um of Art, as well as the likes of the HNM-PCC Hun­gar­i­an Nation­al Muse­um, the Turin Nation­al Uni­ver­si­ty Library, and the Bath Postal Muse­um: insti­tu­tions you can nev­er be sure when you’ll vis­it next. There will, of course, be more muse­ums found­ed in the future. But if things go accord­ing to plan, none of their hold­ings will escape The Last Muse­um’s ever-widen­ing dig­i­tal net. Enter the dig­i­tal col­lec­tion here.

entries.title: How Did Everything Begin?: Animations on the Origins of the Universe Narrated by X‑Files Star Gillian Anderson
entries.summary: We previously brought you the BBC series of short animated videos, A History of Ideas. Produced in collaboration with the UK’s Open University and narrated by Harry Shearer, these fun introductions to such philosophers as Simone de Beauvoir and Edmund Burke, and such weighty philosophical topics as free will and the problem of evil, make […]
entries.content:
We pre­vi­ous­ly brought you the BBC series of short ani­mat­ed videos, A His­to­ry of Ideas. Pro­duced in col­lab­o­ra­tion with the UK’s Open Uni­ver­si­ty and nar­rat­ed by Har­ry Shear­er, these fun intro­duc­tions to such philoso­phers as Simone de Beau­voir and Edmund Burke, and such weighty philo­soph­i­cal top­ics as free will and the prob­lem of evil, make chal­leng­ing, abstract con­cepts acces­si­ble to non-philoso­phers. Now the series is back with a new chap­ter, How Did Every­thing Begin?, a sur­vey of sev­er­al the­o­ries of the ori­gins of the uni­verse, from Thomas Aquinas’ philo­soph­i­cal spec­u­la­tions, to Hin­du cos­mol­o­gy; and from the­olo­gian William Paley’s design argu­ment (below), to the the­o­ry of the Big Bang (above).

The two videos here present an inter­est­ing coun­ter­point between the ori­gin the­o­ries of astro­physics and the­ol­o­gy. Though cur­rent-day intel­li­gent design pro­po­nents deny it, there is still much of William Paley’s argu­ment, at least in style, in their expla­na­tions of cre­ation. First pro­pound­ed in his 1802 work Nat­ur­al The­ol­o­gy, the theologian’s famous watch­mak­er analogy—which he extend­ed to the design of the eye, and every­thing else—gave Charles Dar­win much to puz­zle over, though David Hume had sup­pos­ed­ly refut­ed Paley’s argu­ments 50 years ear­li­er. The Big Bang theory—a term cre­at­ed by its fore­most crit­ic Fred Hoyle—offers an entire­ly nat­u­ral­is­tic account of the universe’s ori­gins, one that pre­sup­pos­es no inher­ent pur­pose or design.

As with the pre­vi­ous videos, these are script­ed by the host of the Phi­los­o­phy Bites pod­cast, Nigel War­bur­ton. This time around the videos are nar­rat­ed by Gillian Ander­son, whose voice you may not imme­di­ate­ly rec­og­nize. Rather than sound­ing like Dana Scul­ly, her famous X‑Files char­ac­ter, Ander­son speaks in a British accent, which she slips into eas­i­ly, hav­ing lived in the UK for much of her child­hood and now again as an adult. (You may have seen Ander­son in many of the Eng­lish peri­od dra­mas she has appeared in, or in British crime dra­ma The Fall or Michael Winterbottom’s uproar­i­ous adap­ta­tion of Tris­tram Shandy.)

These fas­ci­nat­ing spec­u­la­tive theories—whether sci­en­tif­ic or mythological—are sure to appeal to fans of the X‑Files, who can per­haps begin to believe again, or remain skep­ti­cal, thanks to Chris Carter’s R‑rated direc­tor’s cut of X‑Files: I Want to Believe, com­ing out this fall.

Watch the remain­ing videos in the series below:
